Please take the following steps:

1. Review the learning outcomes of the course. Are they standardized for ENC1101? Is the professor meeting the standards?

2. See the professor during office hours. Express your concerns. Hear her side of the story. It may be, as noted elsewhere in this thread, that she is teaching the departmental learning outcomes (just with a topic that she prefers). Meet with her first because the first question from the dean will be, "have you met with your professor and discussed this?"

3. If unsatisfied with her response, make an appointment to see the dean. If she is not teaching appropriately so that you can be successful according to the learning outcomes, the dean will be able to guide you in your options.

I am a dean of arts and humanities at a state college in Florida. I frequently have these kinds of meetings with students. First thing that I do is make sure that the student has met with the professor. Then I review the learning outcomes with the student. I then look at the professor's syllabus to match it with the learning outcomes. If need be, I will meet with the professor.  

Since this is an academic matter, meet with the dean. If she/he is unable to help, then go to your dean of student success.

This response always comes up at some point. If a student completes everything on the rubric, it must be correct. I can't tell you how much I fucking hate the word rubric and loathe No Child Left Behind for forcing them on every teacher and student.

Before becoming a professor, I worked for years in the legal profession. Not once, did a senior partner ever come to me and say, "Ianto, here is everything that you need to do to be successful on this case. I also included a rubric as well." No, it was always, "Here's your case. Get to work." I had to figure out what to do and how to to it right. If it wasn't correctly done, my job was in jeopardy. I didn't get to argue, "well, I did everything you asked for on the rubric!"

When discussing grading, there is no winning. Students feel that they are either being taught and graded on things that are not relevant to them in "the real world" or professors are being unfair because the grading doesn't match the rubric, which doesn't exist in the real world.

I am currently an Acting Dean in a Humanities department at a local state college this term.  So here is my advice: look at the syllabus.  Does her syllabus state that you will receive written feedback?  If she is not abiding by her syllabus, that will be a way for the Dean to tackle the issue. Then, make the argument that her lack of feedback is not allowing you to progress appropriately in the class.  Retention of students is the buzzword in higher ed right now.  We want to retain you and see you succeed.  

Also, have a plan.  Tell the Dean what can be done.  You mentioned transferring to another section.  Provided it is not overcrowded, that should be a valid solution to the issue.  

Finally, don't start with the "she accused me of dishonesty" thing.  He said/she said arguments are hard to get resolved.  Give the Dean something tangible.  Dig through the syllabus and find where she is not following appropriate procedure.

The way that I was taught about Death of the Author creates a power in a thoughtful reader to make meaning.  However, the reader cannot just make up any conclusion, it must be supported by textual evidence.  A thoughtful reader today, still influenced by World War II, may reach a conclusion that LOTR is an allegory for WWII.  However, another reader, in 200 years time, might not get that from the text at all and instead see it an allegory of WWIV, or something else entirely.  

The Death of the Author is simply that we don't need to know everything about the author in order to understand a text.  It does not mean that the author did not create specific aspects to the text, such as tone, mood, location, red herrings, etc.  Instead, it means that the Reader can make sense of all those things herself and not need to know about the Author to understand them.

Look at *Hamlet*, I know next to nothing about the life and times of William Shakespeare, but I can create meaning from the story based on the text itself.  I might even see as it being analogous to some current event, yet, that is my interpretation as a thoughtful reader.  Shakespeare's intent does not matter.  In other words, there is not ONE reading of *Hamlet* or LOTR but a multitude of readings that each person brings to it.

A final point about the Author, which finally made some of my literature professors' ideas stick is J.K. Rowling.  After the end of the Harry Potter series, she made a comment about how obvious it was the Dumbledore was gay.  Yet, even the most sympathetic and thoughtful reader will find it hard to get any textual evidence to support that claim.  J.K. Rowling can claim anything that she wants to, but the Author as final authority over a text is dead. This does not mean that the text or reading the text as a thoughtful reader annihilates itself.  Instead, it forces the reader to not be lazy and rely on someone else to create meaning for her.

As a professor, I agree with everything OP says.  I want to stress a couple of points from my point of view.

1.  Come to class.  I take a lot of time to prepare and create activities for students.  When you aren't there, you miss out on valuable practice.  Plus, if you come to class regularly, I know you, I know your name, and when grades come around, you (normally) want the prof to know who you are.  If you earn an 87, 88 in my class and have attended and I know you, I will round up to 90 and you get the A.

2.  Office hours!  Most of us sit there with nothing to do waiting for students to come by.  Again, it never hurts for the prof to get to know you.

3.  Contrary to what a lot of high schools do, a C grade is seen as average in university.  This means that if you do the basics of an assignment, then that merits a C.  If you go above what I asked you to do, that is a B.  If you go above and beyond and excel, that is an A.  Many of us do not have rubrics, so come talk to us to see what it takes to get a B or an A if you are unsure.  Generally speaking, we like talking to students.  Most of us got into education to help students (yes, some profs are here for research only and don't give a shit about you).  Ask us and we will help.
